Here are my research notes on Leviticus 21, verse by verse. I have gathered material from the sources I could access within the allowed boundaries.

---

## Leviticus 21 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter is divided into three main sections, structured around the "threefold graduation of holiness" — the people, the priests, and the high priest, mirroring the outer court, Holy Place, and Most Holy Place (Enduring Word, citing Rooker; Keil & Delitzsch). It addresses: (1) defilement from the dead and mourning customs (vv. 1–6, 10–12), (2) marriage and family purity (vv. 7–9, 13–15), and (3) physical defects barring priestly service (vv. 16–24).

---

### vv. 1–3 — Prohibition on Defilement for the Dead, with Exceptions

**v. 1: "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Speak to Aaron's sons, the priests, and tell them that a priest is not to defile himself for a dead person among his people…'"**

The Hebrew term translated "defile himself" refers to ceremonial uncleanness. According to Ellicott, the priests' administrators later defined this as including not only touching a dead body but coming within four cubits of it, entering the house where the corpse lay, entering a burial place, following to the grave, or any manifestation of mourning. This was deduced from Numbers 19:11–16. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

Gill notes that the prohibition covered entering a tent where a dead body lay, touching it, bearing it, or attending it to the grave. He adds that the Romans had a similar custom, placing a cypress branch at the door of a house with a dead body so that a chief priest would not unwittingly enter and be defiled. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

Guzik (Enduring Word) explains that a dead body is "a picture of sin's result in this world, especially in the way the body quickly rots." God wanted His priests associated with life, not death, and kept far from pagan death cults. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

Keil & Delitzsch note that the Hebrew word *nephesh* (soul) is used here for a dead person, as in Leviticus 19:28. They explain that since every corpse defiled not only those who touched it but also the tent or dwelling (Numbers 19:14), defilement was unavoidable for the priest as head of the family in cases of family death — hence the exceptions. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

Haydock (Catholic) comments that such regulations were simply "the will of God" — He might intend to exercise their obedience, keep their minds from being too much depressed by the sight of the dead, and remind all to carefully avoid sin, "which kills the soul, and renders us really unclean before God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/21.htm)

**v. 2: "…except for his immediate family—his mother, father, son, daughter, or brother…"**

Gill observes that the wife is not explicitly listed but is understood by many Jewish commentators to be included under "his kin that is near unto him" (rendered "his flesh" by some), since man and wife are one flesh (Genesis 2:24). He notes that the case of Ezekiel (Ezekiel 24:15–17) confirms a priest could mourn his wife; Ezekiel's prohibition was extraordinary, implying it was normally allowed. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch agree: the wife is included *implicite* in "kin that is near unto him," since the wife is not expressly mentioned because man and wife form one flesh, and the wife stands nearer to the husband than father, mother, son, daughter, brother, or sister. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

Ellicott likewise notes that "except for his relatives who are nearest to him" includes the wife, though not explicitly named. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

**v. 3: "…or his unmarried sister who is near to him, since she has no husband."**

Gill: the sister must be a virgin, never betrothed nor married. The "nearness" may refer to nearness of place — being unmarried, she remained in her father's house to her death. If she had a husband, he would be the one to mourn and bury her, so the priest-brother was not needed. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

Ellicott notes the humane dimension: when a corpse was found with no one to bury it, even the priest (or high priest) was obliged to perform the burial himself, per later Jewish authorities. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

---

### v. 4 — The Difficult Verse

**"He is not to defile himself for those related to him by marriage, and so profane himself."**

This is one of the most obscure verses in the chapter. The BSB renders it as a prohibition against defiling oneself for in-laws ("those related to him by marriage"). However, the traditional Hebrew is difficult, and several interpretations compete:

- **Keil & Delitzsch** reject the "in-laws" view and understand v. 4 as a general prohibition heading into vv. 7–9: the priest must not defile himself "as a husband and head of a household" by marrying an immoral wife or training his children carelessly, thus profaning his holy office. They read *ba'al* as "husband / master of the house." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

- **Gill** reports two traditional Jewish views: (a) it means the priest, being a "chief man among his people," must not defile himself for any non-relative, even a ruler — to do so would "profane himself" by making himself unfit for service; (b) some take it as forbidding defilement for a "chief" or principal man among the people. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

- **Haydock (Catholic)** gives the Douay-Rheims rendering: "But not even for the prince of his people shall he be defiled." He notes the alternative reading: "Let not the husband render himself unclean" — some think even the wife is not permitted; this was the view of the Romans, whose priests could not attend their wives' funerals. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/21.htm)

- **Ellicott** says the verse is obscure, and the early translators "wandered in uncertainty among different renderings." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

---

### v. 5 — Pagan Mourning Practices Forbidden

**"Priests must not make bald spots on their heads, shave off the edges of their beards, or make cuts in their bodies."**

Guzik: This same law was given to Israel generally in Leviticus 19:27–28. Both were connected to pagan rites for burial and mourning. The prophets of Baal cut themselves to impress their false god (1 Kings 18:28). Clarke (cited by Guzik) notes that in the apocryphal book of Baruch (6:31), the priests of Babylon sat in their temples "with their clothes rent, and their heads and beards shaven." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

Gill: The Egyptians shaved heads and beards as priests of Isis; Israelites were to be distinct. These were superstitious customs used among the heathen in mourning for the dead, particularly by the Chaldeans. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch: A "constructio ad sensum" in the Hebrew makes the prohibition apply to the whole priestly class. The shaving was done "between the eyes" (Deuteronomy 14:1), as a mourning custom. Herodotus noted that Egyptian priests were shaven, while in other nations, mourners shaved their heads. The Israelites were to be different. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

Haydock: These actions "would indicate an important grief, and want of patience." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/21.htm)

The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary adds: those who live near God's presence, in the joy of His favour, have such consolations in Him as to temper grief — they teach us how to "sorrow not as others who have no hope." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-21.html)

---

### v. 6 — The Rationale: Holiness and the Food of God

**"They must be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God. Because they present to the LORD the offerings made by fire, the food of their God, they must be holy."**

Ellicott: The phrase "the offerings of the LORD made by fire, being the food of God" refers to the altar as God's table and the sacrifice burnt on it as His food (see Leviticus 3:11). Because the priests handle this "food," they must be holy. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

Gill: "The bread of their God" includes both the showbread and all the sacrificial food portions belonging to the priests. Being holy means being "separate from all others" and abstaining from "all impurity both of flesh and spirit." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

Guzik: The phrase "bread of their God" is repeated in v. 8, emphasizing the connection between holiness and fellowship with God. The bread pictured Israel's fellowship with God, as if God and His people shared bread together. The New Testament parallel is 1 John 1:5–6. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

---

### v. 7 — Priestly Marriage Restrictions

**"A priest must not marry a woman defiled by prostitution or divorced by her husband, for the priest is holy to his God."**

Ellicott: From defilement through contact with the dead, the lawgiver passes to the priest's alliances with the living, which "might be fraught with still more serious consequences to his sacred office." The priest must be careful about both chastity and legitimate descent. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

Gill distinguishes the Hebrew terms: *zonah* means a common prostitute; *chalalah* means a woman whose chastity has been violated, whether by force or seduction, but not a professional prostitute. The divorced woman always carried suspicion of something improper, so priests were forbidden to marry such. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch: The priest could only marry a virgin or widow of irreproachable character. She need not be an Israelite by birth but could be the daughter of a stranger living among Israelites — only she must not be an idolater or Canaanite (Exodus 34:16; Deuteronomy 7:3). This contrasts with the high priest (v. 14), who must marry an Israelite virgin. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

Guzik: It is unclear from this verse whether the ordinary priest could marry a widow. The prohibition lists a harlot, a defiled woman, and a divorced woman — widow is not mentioned. However, Ezekiel 44:22 later permits priests to marry "a virgin of the descendants of the house of Israel, or a widow who is the widow of a priest." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

---

### v. 8 — The People's Duty to Regard the Priest as Holy

**"You are to regard him as holy, since he presents the food of your God. He shall be holy to you, because I the LORD am holy—I who set you apart."**

Gill: This is addressed to Moses and the civil magistrates in succession. "Thou shalt sanctify him" means to esteem and reckon him a holy person, to preserve him from impurity, and even — as Jarchi said — "whether he will or not; if he will not put her away, beat him and chastise him until he does put her away." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch: "Thou shalt sanctify him" means not merely "respect his holy dignity" but take active care that he does not desecrate his office by a polluted marriage. The Israelites as a nation are addressed in the persons of their chiefs. The repetition ("he shall be holy unto thee") strengthens the exhortation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

---

### v. 9 — The Priest's Daughter Who Becomes a Prostitute

**"If a priest's daughter defiles herself by prostituting herself, she profanes her father; she must be burned in the fire."**

Gill: This is an aggravation — the daughter of a priest had the honour of her father's sacred office, the advantage of a more strictly religious education, and had eaten of the holy things. Her sin brings disgrace on her father's name and office. Burning with fire (not stoning) was the punishment — possibly because it was more terrible. The man who lay with her was, according to the Mishnah, to be strangled. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch: "She profaned her father" — the priest-man (*kōhēn 'îš*). She was to be burned, i.e., stoned and then burned (see Leviticus 20:14 on the order of execution). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

Rooker (cited in Enduring Word): "A priest who would allow a prostitute to reside under his roof would not be qualified to render decisions on behalf of the covenant community." Guzik notes the New Testament parallel: a leader must manage his household well (1 Timothy 3:4–5; Titus 1:6). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

Haydock: If she is betrothed and still in her father's house, the infamy falls upon him; if she is with her husband, she undergoes the usual punishment of stoning. Other young women received no corporal punishment for simple fornication — the man was bound to marry them or pay a dowry (Exodus 22:16). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/21.htm)

---

### v. 10 — The High Priest: Hair and Garments

**"The priest who is highest among his brothers, who has had the anointing oil poured on his head and has been ordained to wear the priestly garments, must not let his hair hang loose or tear his garments."**

Guzik: This is the first place in the Bible where the title "high priest" appears — Clarke calls it "very emphatic, *haccohen haggadol*, that priest, the great one." The high priest is distinct in his anointing and garments (Exodus 28:1–30). Jesus is a High Priest, but after the order of Melchizedek, not Aaron (Hebrews 5:1–11). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

Ellicott: "Shall not uncover his head" is better rendered "shall not let his head be dishevelled" — a sign of mourning (see Leviticus 10:6). Jonathan's Targum adds "in the time of distress," meaning as an expression of sorrow. Sustaining this high position as intercessor between God and man, such outward expressions might lead people to believe he impugns the justice of the Divine judgment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

Gill: The high priest must not take off his mitre, or let his hair grow long for mourning (more than thirty days, per rabbinic tradition). He may rend his clothes for blasphemy (as Caiaphas did in Matthew 26:65), but not for the dead. Jewish canons permitted the high priest to rend his garments only "below, near his feet," whereas a common priest rends above. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

---

### v. 11 — The High Priest and the Dead, Even Parents

**"He must not go near any dead body; he must not defile himself, even for his father or mother."**

Gill: If the high priest may not defile himself for his parents, it follows he certainly may not for son, daughter, brother, or sister (the exceptions for the common priest in vv. 2–3). One exception made by later Jewish authorities: if the high priest met an unburied corpse on the road with no one to bury it, he was obliged to defile himself and bury it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: The ordinary priests were allowed, when death fell on their nearest relationships, to relax their ministries for a while — but not so the high priest. His absence from the tabernacle would arrest all the services of the sanctuary, and his contact with the dead would disqualify him to intercede for the people before God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-21.html)

---

### v. 12 — The High Priest Must Not Leave the Sanctuary

**"He must not leave or desecrate the sanctuary of his God, for the consecration of the anointing oil of his God is on him. I am the LORD."**

Ellicott: When tidings of a parent's death reached the high priest during his service, he must not desist and quit the sanctuary, "lest it should appear that he has a greater regard for the dead than for the service of the living God." The difference: a common priest who heard of a death during service was *obliged* to discontinue (though he could not leave the precincts); the high priest *never became a mourner* and so profaned the service if he discontinued it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch: This does not mean the sanctuary was his constant abode (as some have maintained). It means he was not to go out *funeris causa* — for the sake of a funeral. The word *nēzer* here means consecration, not the diadem (as in Exodus 29:6). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

Grant's Commentary: This must be true "so long as he was acting in the capacity of high priest." So today, the Lord Jesus has entered the holy place (heaven itself) once and maintains His service for His saints there (Hebrews 9:11–12). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-21.html)

Haydock adds a pastoral note: "Priests must be detached, as much as possible, from all things which might divert them from their sacred offices. The greatest holiness is required of those who receive the body of Jesus Christ." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/21.htm)

---

### vv. 13–14 — The High Priest's Marriage

**"The woman he marries must be a virgin. He is not to marry a widow, a divorced woman, or one defiled by prostitution. He is to marry a virgin from his own people…"**

Ellicott notes four requirements deduced by administrators of the Law during the Second Temple: (1) the high priest must be the husband of one wife (ordinary priests might have several); (2) she must be a virgin under age thirteen; (3) she must not even have been betrothed to another; (4) she must be the daughter of Jewish parents by race — the LXX adds "of his own race." St. Paul enjoins the first on Christian bishops (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch: Unlike the common priest (who could marry a non-Israelite of good character), the high priest must marry "a virgin of his own people" — an Israelitish woman only. *Zonah* (whore) is in apposition to *chalalah* (fallen woman), meaning a fallen woman was equivalent to a whore for him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

Haydock: Josephus says the high priest could not divorce her. The Rabbis allowed him only one wife. The Egyptian priests, according to Diodorus, also married only one wife. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/21.htm)

---

### v. 15 — Not Defiling His Offspring

**"…so that he does not defile his offspring among his people, for I am the LORD who sanctifies him."**

Keil & Delitzsch: "Neither shall he profane his seed (posterity) among his people" — by contracting a marriage not in keeping with the holiness of his rank. The children of an unlawful marriage would be disqualified from the priesthood. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

Guzik: The high priest also had to raise his children before the LORD and not profane them "by any dedication or service to the pagan gods of the surrounding nations." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

---

### vv. 16–21 — Physical Defects Barring Priestly Service

**v. 17: "…none of your descendants who has a physical defect may approach to offer the food of his God."**

Ellicott: Having covered voluntary disqualifications (mourning customs, illegal marriages), the legislator now passes to blemishes that, "though not voluntarily contracted, likewise disqualify the priests for performing sacerdotal duties." During the Second Temple, authorities registered no fewer than 142 defects that disqualified a priest. A special chamber in the Temple court was used by the Sanhedrin to examine priests: those disqualified "put on black garments … and went away in silence"; those qualified celebrated with a feast. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown): "As visible things exert a strong influence on the minds of men, any physical infirmity or malformation … which disturbs the associations or excites ridicule, tends to detract from the weight and authority of the sacred office." In all these regulations there was a "typical reference to the priesthood of Christ (Hebrews 7:26)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/leviticus/21.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch: "As the spiritual nature of a man is reflected in his bodily form, only a faultless condition of body could correspond to the holiness of the priest; just as the Greeks and Romans required … that the priests should be ὁλόκληροι, *integri corporis*" (Plato *De Legibus* 6.759; Plutarch *Quaest. Rom.* 73). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

Guzik: The "perfection" required in both sacrifice and priest was only comparative, not absolute. The combination of perfect offering (1 Peter 1:19) and perfect offerer (Hebrews 7:26) was fulfilled in Jesus Christ. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

**v. 18:** "…blind, lame, disfigured, or deformed" — Keil & Delitzsch parse *charum* as one with a mutilated face (nose, ears, lips, or eyes), not merely a flat nose. *Sāruaʿ* means "stretched out" — a limb too long or an ill-formed member, possibly extra fingers/toes (2 Samuel 21:20). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

**v. 19:** "…broken foot or hand" — Keil & Delitzsch: a fracture. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

**v. 20:** "…hunchback or dwarf, or who has an eye defect, a festering rash, scabs, or a crushed testicle" — Keil & Delitzsch: *dāq* ("dwarf") means one with an unnaturally thin or withered body. *Gārāb* is "the itch"; *yallephet* is "ringworm." *Merōaḥ āšek* ("crushed testicle") does not mean castration (prohibited in Deuteronomy 23:2) but one with crushed or softened stones. The LXX renders it μόνορχις (having only one testicle). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

**v. 21:** "…Since he has a defect, he is not to come near to offer the food of his God." — The summary statement shows the list was representative, not exhaustive. The administrators of the Law were to determine other cases. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

Rooker (cited in Guzik): In inter-testamental days, Antigonus had the ears of the high priest Hyrcanus II cut off so that he would forever be disqualified from the high priesthood under this law. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

---

### vv. 22–23 — The Blemished Priest May Still Eat the Holy Food

**v. 22: "He may eat the most holy food of his God as well as the holy food…"**

Gill and Ellicott both stress this merciful provision: though unfit for serving at the altar, the blemished priest was allowed to partake of the less holy sacrificial gifts (peace offerings, tithes, first-fruits) and also the most holy portions (what remained of the meat-offerings, sin-offerings, and trespass-offerings). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

Guzik: This shows that "involuntary weakness doesn't bar us from God's care." Trapp is quoted: "Our involuntary weaknesses shall not debar us from benefit by Christ." Though Yahweh was still "his God," the blemished priest was excluded only from specific priestly service, not from relationship. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

Grant's Commentary (Brethren): Physical defects are "typical of spiritual or moral defects, of which there were none in the Lord Jesus." A believer with moral or spiritual "defects" may eat the bread of his God but is "disqualified from public service." Mephibosheth is an example of one who ate at the king's table despite his lameness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-21.html)

**v. 23: "…because he has a defect, he must not go near the veil or approach the altar, so as not to desecrate My sanctuaries."**

Ellicott: "go in unto the veil" means entering the holy place which was before the veil — to light the lamps, burn incense, or set out the showbread. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/leviticus/21.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch: the prohibition is so that the blemished priest "might not desecrate the sanctuary of the Lord." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary describes the threefold practical principle: (1) Defilement disqualifies for near fellowship; (2) Defect disqualifies for highest service; (3) Yet there remains for the weak and defective a relationship with Christ — "He shall eat the bread of his God: only he shall not go in unto the veil." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-21.html)

---

### v. 24 — Moses Delivers the Instructions

**"Moses told this to Aaron and his sons and to all the Israelites."**

Keil & Delitzsch simply note: "Moses communicated these instructions to Aaron and his sons." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html) The public proclamation to "all the Israelites" (noted by Guzik) underscores that the whole nation was to hold the priests to these standards. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### On Physical Defects and Church Leadership (vv. 16–23)

- **Reformed/Presbyterian (typified by JFB):** Emphasizes the typical reference to Christ — as the sacrifice had to be without blemish, so the priest had to be without blemish, both pointing to Christ's perfection (Hebrews 7:26). Physical requirements in the Old Testament foreshadow moral and spiritual perfection in the New. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/leviticus/21.htm)

- **Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Stresses that bodily perfection reflects spiritual nature — "as the spiritual nature of a man is reflected in his bodily form." They note the parallel with Greek and Roman priestly requirements, seeing a universal religious intuition at work. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word):** Strongly emphasizes that the blemished priest could still "eat the bread of his God," making the point that involuntary weakness does not bar anyone from God's care or relationship. The emphasis falls on grace within boundaries. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

- **Brethren (Grant):** Reads the physical defects as strictly typical of "spiritual or moral defects." A believer with moral failings is disqualified from public service but may still eat. The typology is pressed into present-day church order. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-21.html)

- **Methodist/Wesleyan/Holiness (Preacher's Homiletical Commentary):** Highlights that "physical malformations necessarily unfit men for solemn public offices when they attract observation, disturb reverence, and induce ridicule" — yet within a deformed body "may dwell a beautiful soul." The emphasis is pastoral: the blemished are not excluded from "gracious and loving work in the Church." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-21.html)

### On v. 4 (the Obscure Verse)

- **Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Understood as a heading to the marriage laws in vv. 7–9 — the priest as "husband and head of a household" must not defile himself. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-21.html)

- **Baptist (Gill, following rabbinic sources):** Understood as forbidding defilement even for a "chief man" or ruler among the people who was not a relative. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/21.htm)

- **Catholic (Haydock/Douay):** Rendered "not even for the prince of his people shall he be defiled," but acknowledges alternative interpretations including the husband/wife question. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/21.htm)

---

## Catholic and Orthodox Readings

### Catholic (Haydock / Douay-Rheims)

The Catholic reading emphasizes the typological application to Christian priesthood. Haydock repeatedly draws lessons for Christian priests: "Let Christian priests hence learn what sanctity will be required of them." The high priest's prohibition from burying even his father prompts the question — answered by St. Augustine — that the high priest was to be consecrated immediately after his father's death to offer incense; another could perform the burial. The physical blemishes of the old law "were figures of the vices which priests are to beware of in the new law" (St. Gregory, *Cura Pastoralis*). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/leviticus/21.htm)

The Douay-Rheims renders v. 4 as "Nay, he must not expose himself to defilement even for the ruler among the people," with a footnote marking textual uncertainty. V. 15 in the Douay reads: "so that the stock of his family is not debased by the blood of common folk." This reflects the LXX tradition that the high priest's wife must be "of his own race." (https://www.newadvent.org/bible/lev021.htm)

## Summary of Christological Typology (across traditions)

Virtually all the commentators agree on the central typology: the perfect priest and the perfect sacrifice both point to Jesus Christ. As Guzik summarizes: "The combination of a perfect sacrifice and a perfect priest, both without blemish, points to Jesus Christ, who is both the perfect offering and the perfect offerer." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-21/)

The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: "Our Divine Priest was in all points perfect — 'without blemish'; in Him God was 'well pleased.' No defect mars His acceptance as He appears in the presence of God for us … He is the faultless Jesus; 'fairest among ten thousand, and altogether lovely.'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/leviticus-21.html)

Grant's Commentary: The high priest's bride must be a virgin of his own people — so "the Bride of Christ, the Church, is considered 'not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing' (Ephesians 5:27), and is only from the family of faith." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/leviticus-21.html)
